doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Deciding to write: his father, school papers, Syracuse and the AACM liner-note writers
summary: His father's encouragement, early newspapers, college counterculture editing and pop listening, and the draw of writing about AACM music and the challenge of describing sound.

venues.name: Ann Arbor Blues and Jazz Festival

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: What inspired you to pursue a career as a writer?

Well I kind of have to give my dad a lot of appreciation for encouraging that. At one point a conversation I remember well, he and I were driving and he said have you thought about what you want to do when you grow up? I was maybe twelve or thirteen. And I said I don’t know. And he said well when I was your age I wanted to be a writer. And again I thought that’s okay? That would be okay? So he said to me at the time, the people who you’re reading though, most of them were reporters first, and many of them were sports writers. I was reading Damon Runyon and Ring Lardner and also P.G. Wodehouse who I don’t think was a sports writer. But I had very little interest in sports. I was a Cubs fan and they always seemed to be more like the Marx brothers than like a professional sports team. So I thought well I’m not too interested in sports but I could write about the movies, I could write about books. And I wrote about culture, I had a little newspaper when I was in sixth grade where I wrote movie reviews for my own little newspaper that © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

I was putting out. I was on the high school newspaper. And when we moved to the suburbs that was pretty good actually journalistic training. It was a weekly paper and it was substantial for a high school paper. And when I was in college also I was the counterculture editor of the college paper for a while, in Syracuse University. And of course there was a big explosion of music in the late sixties, and I did connect with pop music at that time, Jimi Hendrix, Aretha Franklin, Motown and some rock & roll, “Surrealistic Pillow” the Jefferson Airplane. I liked anything that was out. Anything that seemed psychological or seemed surreal was of interest to me. So some of the San Francisco bands like Quicksilver Messenger Service I remember I liked a lot. And the blues stuff from Chicago, even on the white side, Mike Bloomfield and Paul Butterfield. So that interested me. And more so than the British invasion. And of course it became possible to write about music. It seemed like especially the AACM music that I was hearing. I didn’t see many people in the audience who would be in a position to write about it. I wasn’t reading much about it. Terry Martin, John Litweiler and J.B. Fighy, the guys who were writing the liner notes for the Delmark records that were coming out were the only people who seemed to be acknowledging this music, which I just found fascinating. And I thought I could write something about this. If I just really concentrate on what I can be sure I know, and transmit just that, and try not to speculate and try not to put critical judgements on it that are — it was subject matter to me that I could express verbally on the page. And it seemed very dramatic. And of course you know when you’re young if you want to be a writer, you really don’t have much to write about. You can write about yourself and your teenage angst or something and I shunned that idea. And then I didn’t have anything else to write about. So here was something that was not me but I was interested in and seemed so inherently dramatic. And the challenge of writing about sound. We can’t see it, you can’t touch it, so how do you describe it to somebody else in a way that’s going to convey the sense of it. And that became — it was a challenge and I was interested in it and I began to focus on it. And I had a little bit of success in placing some articles. And I think it just was because I pursued listening to it so avidly. I went to the Ann Arbor blues and jazz festivals, I worked at the Jazz Record Mart in Chicago so I met several musicians.
